Samsung Electronics), the Federal Circuit held that a claim covering a scientifically impossible alternative embodiment may be clear, i.e., definite in its scope, but because an impossible alternative embodiment cannot be made or used, its inclusion may render the claim invalid for lack of enablement.
In 2018, Satius Holding (Satius) sued Samsung Electronics (Samsung) in the district court of Delaware, alleging infringement of claims 1, 11, and 18 of U.S. Patent No. 6,711,385, which concerns a coupler for wireless communications.
In Samsung’s view, the phrase “communicating electric signals to the air” merely indicates that electric signals can pass through the communications apparatus. The phrase does not mean electric signals can propagate through the air, as the phrase “over air” would otherwise suggest. See Satius Holding, Inc.

exa.snippet:
October 23, 2026 

 Authored and Edited by Erin M. Lynch; Christopher B. Anderson; Erik R. Puknys 

In Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd., No. 25-1446 (Fed. Cir. Oct. 1, 2026), the Federal Circuit affirmed an invalidity finding for Satius’ U.S. Patent No. 6,711,385 but did so on enablement grounds rather than the indefiniteness grounds relied on by the district court. 

Satius sued Samsung for infringement of the ’385 patent, which claims a communications apparatus capable of transmitting electric (along with electromagnetic) signals over air—a feat that both parties agreed is scientifically impossible. As a result, the district court held the asserted claims indefinite and entered a final judgment of invalidity in favor of Samsung. Satius appealed, challenging the finding of indefiniteness. In reply, Samsung argued that the claims were invalid for lack of enablement even if found to be definite.

On appeal, the Federal Circuit rejected the district court's indefiniteness ruling, holding that, despite the scientific impossibility of transmitting electric signals over air, the claims still allow a skilled artisan to understand the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty, thus satisfying the definiteness requirement. The Court nevertheless affirmed invalidity on enablement grounds, exercising its discretion to reach the issue because it had been fully briefed on appeal. Emphasizing that § 112(a) requires the specification to enable the full scope of the claims, the Court held that claims encompassing a scientifically impossible embodiment are inoperable and therefore not enabled.

by Dennis Crouch

The Federal Circuit has affirmed invalidity of Satius's wireless-coupler patent, but on a different ground than the district court. Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., No. 2025-1446 (Fed. Cir. Oct. 1, 2026). Claim 1 of U.S. Patent No. 6,711,385 recites an apparatus "for transmitting electric or electromagnetic signals over air." Everyone agrees the first option is impossible: electromagnetic signals travel through air; electric signals do not. Magistrate Judge Burke (D. Del.) held the claims indefinite on that basis. Chief Judge Moore's opinion for the panel (joined by Judges Lourie and Hughes) rejects that reasoning, holding that a claim can be clear about its scope even when part of that scope is physically impossible. The court then held the claims invalid for lack of enablement, an issue the district court had found waived.

Judge Hughes previewed the result at oral argument: "If I claim the transporter from Star Trek, everybody knows what I'm claiming. It's impossible. But it's impossible because it's not enabled, not because it's indefinite." The panel's precedential opinion adopts that view.

Federal Circuit Affirms Invalidity Challenge to Scientifically Impossible Claim Language on Enablement Grounds

October 23, 2026
Authored and Edited by Erin M. Lynch ; Christopher B. Anderson ; Erik R. Puknys
In Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd., No. 25-1446 (Fed. Cir. Oct. 1, 2026) , the Federal Circuit affirmed an invalidity finding for Satius’ U.S. Patent No. 6,711,385 but did so on enablement grounds rather than the indefiniteness grounds relied on by the district court.
Satius sued Samsung for infringement of the ’385 patent, which claims a communications apparatus capable of transmitting electric (along with electromagnetic) signals over air—a feat that both parties agreed is scientifically impossible. As a result, the district court held the asserted claims indefinite and entered a final judgment of invalidity in favor of Samsung. Satius appealed, challenging the finding of indefiniteness. In reply, Samsung argued that the claims were invalid for lack of enablement even if found to be definite.
On appeal, the Federal Circuit rejected the district court's indefiniteness ruling, holding that, despite the scientific impossibility of transmitting electric signals over air, the claims still allow a skilled artisan to understand the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty, thus satisfying the definiteness requirement. The Court nevertheless affirmed invalidity on enablement grounds, exercising its discretion to reach the issue because it had been fully briefed on appeal. Emphasizing that § 112(a) requires the specification to enable the full scope of the claims, the Court held that claims encompassing a scientifically impossible embodiment are inoperable and therefore not enabled.

On October 1, 2026, the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit clarified the interplay between the indefiniteness and enablement requirements on review of a judgment of invalidity due to an “impossible” claim limitation. seltz.title: Federal Circuit Affirms Invalidity Challenge to Scientifically Impossible Claim Language on Enablement Grounds
seltz.snippet:
In *Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.,* No. 25-1446 (Fed. Cir. Oct. 1, 2026), the Federal Circuit affirmed an invalidity finding for Satius’ U.S. Patent No. 6,711,385 but did so on enablement grounds rather than the indefiniteness grounds relied on by the district court. 

Satius sued Samsung for infringement of the ’385 patent, which claims a communications apparatus capable of transmitting electric (along with electromagnetic) signals over air—a feat that both parties agreed is scientifically impossible. As a result, the district court held the asserted claims indefinite and entered a final judgment of invalidity in favor of Samsung. Satius appealed, challenging the finding of indefiniteness. In reply, Samsung argued that the claims were invalid for lack of enablement even if found to be definite.

On appeal, the Federal Circuit rejected the district court's indefiniteness ruling, holding that, despite the scientific impossibility of transmitting electric signals over air, the claims still allow a skilled artisan to understand the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty, thus satisfying the definiteness requirement. The Court nevertheless affirmed invalidity on enablement grounds, exercising its discretion to reach the issue because it had been fully briefed on appeal. Emphasizing that § 112(a) requires the specification to enable the full scope of the claims, the Court held that claims encompassing a scientifically impossible embodiment are inoperable and therefore not enabled.

seltz.title: Clear but Impossible: Satius v. Samsung Moves Inoperable Claims from Indefiniteness to Enablement
seltz.snippet:
by Dennis Crouch

The Federal Circuit has affirmed invalidity of Satius's wireless-coupler patent, but on a different ground than the district court. *Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co.*, No. 2025-1446 (Fed. Cir. Oct. 1, 2026). Claim 1 of U.S. Patent No. 6,711,385 recites an apparatus \"for transmitting electric or electromagnetic signals over air.\" Everyone agrees the first option is impossible: electromagnetic signals travel through air; electric signals do not. Magistrate Judge Burke (D. Del.) held the claims indefinite on that basis. Chief Judge Moore's opinion for the panel (joined by Judges Lourie and Hughes) rejects that reasoning, holding that a claim can be clear about its scope even when part of that scope is physically impossible. The court then held the claims invalid for lack of enablement, an issue the district court had found waived.

Judge Hughes previewed the result at oral argument: \"If I claim the transporter from Star Trek, everybody knows what I'm claiming. It's impossible. But it's impossible because it's not enabled, not because it's indefinite.\" The panel's precedential opinion adopts that view.

webiq.title: Satius v. Samsung (2026) — video case brief | Goodhue, Coleman & Owens, P.C.
webiq.snippet:
In Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., No. 2025-1446 (Fed. Cir. Oct. 1, 2026), the Federal Circuit, in an opinion by Chief Judge Moore, held that claims reciting an apparatus for transmitting "electric" signals over air — an undisputed scientific impossibility — were not indefinite, because their scope was clear. The court nonetheless affirmed the judgment of invalidity on the alternative ground of lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 (a): the specification must enable the full scope of the claims, and an inoperable alternative cannot be made or used. ... Satius Holding v. Samsung Electronics, decided October 1st, 2026. A precedential panel of the Federal Circuit, in an opinion by Chief Judge Moore, held that a patent claim covering a scientific impossibility is not, for that reason, indefinite. But the same claim is invalid for lack of enablement, because no one can make or use an embodiment that cannot exist. The court affirmed the judgment of invalidity on that alternative ground.  ... Claim 1 covers an apparatus for transmitting electric or electromagnetic signals over air. The parties agreed that transmitting a signal over air in electric form is scientifically impossible. On that basis, the district court held all three claims indefinite and entered judgment of invalidity. Satius appealed. Samsung defended the judgment and argued, in the alternative, that the claims were not enabled.

Satius argued that the preamble really described an electric signal converted into an electromagnetic one before it left the device. The court disagreed. Transmitting signals over the air is not the same as transmitting them to the air, and a court may not redraft claims to make them operable or to sustain their validity.

you.title: Satius Holding v. Samsung Electronics: Impossible Claims Can Still ...
you.snippet:
On October 1, 2026, the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit clarified the interplay between the indefiniteness and enablement requirements on review of a judgment of invalidity due to an “impossible” claim limitation. In Satius Holding v. Samsung Electronics, the Court concluded that a claim that includes a scientific impossibility may still be definite if it informs with reasonable certainty the scope of the invention.
See Satius Holding, Inc. v. Samsung Elecs. Co., Appeal No. 2025-1446, at *4 (Fed. Cir. Oct. 1, 2026). The Federal Circuit, however, was unconvinced, finding that Satius’s proposed interpretation would contradict the general assumption that “different terms have different meanings” and would “require rewriting claim 1 to provide for an electric-to-electromagnetic transformation step” that does not exist in the claim language.

you.title: Clearly Impossible: Federal Circuit Issues Precedential Ruling ...
you.snippet:
In a recent precedential decision that came out on October 1, 2026 (Satius Holding v. Samsung Electronics), the Federal Circuit held that a claim covering a scientifically impossible alternative embodiment may be clear, i.e., definite in its scope, but because an impossible alternative embodiment cannot be made or used, its inclusion may render the claim invalid for lack of enablement.
In 2018, Satius Holding (Satius) sued Samsung Electronics (Samsung) in the district court of Delaware, alleging infringement of claims 1, 11, and 18 of U.S. Patent No. 6,711,385, which concerns a coupler for wireless communications.
In Samsung’s view, the phrase “communicating electric signals to the air” merely indicates that electric signals can pass through the communications apparatus. The phrase does not mean electric signals can propagate through the air, as the phrase “over air” would otherwise suggest. See Satius Holding, Inc.
On appeal, Satius argued that the district court erred in holding claims 1, 11, and 18 indefinite. Samsung defended the indefiniteness ruling. In the alternative, Samsung argued that the claims were invalid for lack of enablement. See Satius Holding, LLC, FKA Satius Holding, Inc.
